period.label: Fuente y Caudal / flamenco rumba modernization (1973)

position_in_era.primary_genre_lineage: flamenco rumba × Latin/jazz instrumentation (commercial breakthrough of modern flamenco)
position_in_era.historical_role: An improvised flamenco rumba — recorded almost as filler at producer José Torregrosa's last-minute request — that crossed over to mainstream Spanish listeners (300,000 copies of *Fuente y Caudal*) and made flamenco internationally legible. The first widely-heard flamenco recording with congas, bongos, and electric bass; replaced traditional palmas with bongo on a flagship track. Both modernization and commercial-canonization root for everything Dorantes' generation built on.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded 1973, released on the album *Fuente y Caudal* on Philips/Polygram Spain. Produced by José Torregrosa, who told Paco the album was incomplete and needed one more piece — *Entre dos aguas* was improvised in the session.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Paco de Lucía is the figure Dorantes' jazz-piano colleague Chano Domínguez later called 'his biggest influence along with Bill Evans' — Paco's modernization made flamenco-jazz piano thinkable as a project.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Spain in 1973, two years before Franco's death; the piece functioned as a quiet manifesto that flamenco could change without dissolving.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Flamenco guitar (Paco) plus congas, bongos, electric bass — instruments that were unheard of in flamenco recordings before this.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Improvised in studio under deadline pressure; became the breakout commercial hit of Paco's career and one of the most-played flamenco pieces in mainstream Spanish radio.
